---
title: "Choosing a design"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 110)
```

A simulation study gives you a table of designs and their average outcomes.
This article is about turning that table into a decision. Real decisions
rarely have one goal: you want more gain, *and* lower cost, *and* enough
genetic diversity left for the future. tidyagsim has a helper for each way of
weighing those goals, and each is shown here with a picture.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyagsim)
library(AlphaSimR)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## The question

A recurrent selection program runs ten cycles. Each cycle we grow and measure
`progeny` plants at 15 dollars a plot and intermate the best `n_select`.
Which combination should we run?

```{r}
recurrent <- alphasim_program(
  function(founders, SP, n_select, progeny, cycles) {
    tracker <- asr_tracker(founders)
    pop <- founders
    for (cycle in seq_len(cycles)) {
      pop <- setPheno(pop)
      parents <- selectInd(pop, n_select)
      pop <- randCross(parents, nCrosses = progeny)
      tracker$record(pop, year = cycle, cost = progeny * 15)
    }
    asr_summary(tracker)
  },
  n_select = tune(), progeny = tune(), cycles = 10,
  founders = asr_founders(n_founders = 200, n_chr = 10, seg_sites = 100, plot_h2 = 0.3),
  params = list(n_select = sim_param(c(4, 60), label = "Parents kept"),
                progeny = sim_param(c(100, 600), label = "Plants per cycle")),
  check = function(n_select, progeny) if (n_select > progeny / 2) "Keep at most half the plants."
)

metrics <- sim_metric_set(release_gain, cost, genetic_variance)
```

The `check` function marks impossible designs, so tuners skip them. The
metric set lists what we care about, and says which direction is better for
each: more gain, lower cost, more genetic variance left.

## Run a grid

```{r}
grid <- expand.grid(n_select = c(5, 10, 20, 40), progeny = c(100, 200, 400))
res <- tune_grid(recurrent, sim_replicates(20, seed = 1), grid = grid, metrics = metrics)
res
```

Twelve designs, twenty replicates each, and one line of code. A heat map
shows the whole table at once:

```{r, fig.alt = "Heat map of gain after ten cycles by parents kept and plants per cycle. Gain rises with plants per cycle and peaks at 10 to 20 parents."}
wide <- collect_metrics(res, type = "wide")
ggplot(wide, aes(factor(n_select), factor(progeny), fill = release_gain)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", release_gain)), colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(end = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "Parents kept", y = "Plants per cycle", fill = "Gain",
       title = "Gain after ten cycles (founder genetic SDs)")
```

## Four ways to pick

**1. Just the best.** `show_best()` ranks by one metric:

```{r}
show_best(res, metric = "release_gain", n = 3)
```

**2. The best you can afford.** Constraints filter designs by their *average*
outcomes before ranking. With a total budget of 30,000 dollars:

```{r}
show_best(res, metric = "release_gain", constraints = list(cost = 30000), n = 3)
```

**3. The cheapest that is nearly the best.** The top designs' averages are
often within Monte Carlo error of each other. The *one standard error rule*
takes the best design's average minus one standard error as "good enough",
and picks the cheapest design that reaches it:

```{r}
select_by_one_std_err(res, cost, metric = "release_gain")
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Gain against cost for all designs with error bars. A dashed line marks one standard error below the best design; only the best design itself is above it, and it is highlighted."}
best <- show_best(res, metric = "release_gain", n = 1)
bar <- best$mean - best$std_err
pick <- select_by_one_std_err(res, cost, metric = "release_gain")
wide$picked <- wide$.config == pick$.config
ggplot(wide, aes(cost, release_gain)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = bar, linetype = 2) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = release_gain - release_gain_se, ymax = release_gain + release_gain_se,
                      colour = picked)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey50", `TRUE` = "#E45756"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Total cost (dollars)", y = "Gain after ten cycles",
       title = "The one-standard-error rule",
       subtitle = "Dashed: best design minus one SE. Red: cheapest design at or above it.")
```

Here the rule picks the best design itself. No cheaper design comes within
one standard error of it, so in this program the extra plants are worth
paying for. With a flatter response, the rule would point to a cheaper design
and save money for almost no loss in gain.

**4. The trade-off itself.** Gain now and diversity for later pull against
each other, and no single number settles that. The *Pareto front* lists the
designs that no other design beats on both at once. Every other design is
dominated, meaning something else is at least as good on both:

```{r}
pareto_front(res, metrics = c("release_gain", "genetic_variance"))
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Gain against remaining genetic variance for each design, with the Pareto front highlighted."}
autoplot(res, type = "pareto", metric = c("release_gain", "genetic_variance"))
```

The front is a menu, not an answer. A program with a long horizon might pick
from its diverse end, and a program that must release a variety in five years
might pick from its high-gain end. The decision is yours, and the picture
makes it an informed one.

## Searching larger spaces

A grid of twelve designs is easy to run in full. With more settings, or wider
ranges, the grid grows quickly. Two smarter searches cut the work.

**Racing** runs every design on a few replicates, then drops the ones that
are clearly worse than the leader before running more:

```{r}
race <- tune_race(recurrent, sim_replicates(20, seed = 1), grid = 16, metrics = metrics,
                  burn_in = 4)
race
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Racing plot: designs still in the race against replicates simulated. Most designs are dropped right after the first few replicates."}
autoplot(race, type = "race")
```

The race used `r nrow(race$raw)` simulations, compared with
`r 16 * 20` for the full grid.

**Bayesian optimization** fits a statistical model to the designs it has run
and uses it to choose the next design to try. It can respect constraints too,
here the highest gain within the 30,000 dollar budget:

```{r}
bo <- tune_bayes(recurrent, sim_replicates(10, seed = 1), metrics = metrics,
                 constraints = list(cost = 30000), initial = 6, iter = 10)
show_best(bo, metric = "release_gain", constraints = list(cost = 30000), n = 3)
```

## Summary

| Question | Helper |
|---|---|
| Which design is best on one metric? | `show_best()`, `select_best()` |
| Best within a budget or other limit? | `show_best(constraints = )` |
| Cheapest design that is about as good as the best? | `select_by_one_std_err()`, `select_by_pct_loss()` |
| Which designs are worth considering when goals conflict? | `pareto_front()`, `autoplot(type = "pareto")` |
| Is design B really better than design A? | `compare_designs()` |
| Too many designs to run them all? | `tune_race()`, `tune_bayes()` |
